Sir, thank you so much for being here. Welcome to Miespropius Finances. How are you doing?
Well, Juan and Alejandro, I'm excited to be here with you guys, and looking forward to the session.
Well, we've been waiting for this interview for more than a year.

And one of the things, Monish, let me start by saying, one of the things that I admire the most

showing up, giving us our time, giving the time to our community.

Well, you know, the tone was set by Ben Graham and Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger.
You know, Buffett says that on his gravestone, he just wants it written that he was a teacher.
We are just trying to follow some of those great ideals, which I think is wonderful.
Awesome. Well, now that you mentioned Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger,
and we talked to you this year at the conference in Omaha, Nebraska,
and we asked you how much did you pay to have lunch with Warren Buffett? And you told me you paid
$650,000. What was going through your mind when you signed that check to have lunch with one of your
your idols, Warren Buffett? Well, actually, it turned out to be quite a bar.
It was even even at that time in 2007. So I had bid for the lunch a few years before
that, but I always lost. You know, somebody else outbid me. 2007 was a big year in terms of our returns and fees

So if someone made you, you know, $70, $80 million, you know, what would you
think is an appropriate tuition bill to pay? I thought for sure a couple of million dollars is not a problem.
I was mentally prepared in 2007 when we were bidding to go up to $2 million for the lunch.
And then, you know, because you have like seven seats at the table and I was going to go
with my family, there were three seats open. So I was thinking, you know, should I
take somebody else or if you just keep it with the family. I don't even know now
why I asked him, but I only asked one person if they wanted to join me because, you know, I wanted to make sure
it was someone I would enjoy, you know, breaking bread with. And so I asked Guy Spear if he's interested
in, you know, bidding on the lunch with me. To my surprise, he said, yeah, that sounds great. So
I said, look, you're only going to be two of you and there are four of us.
So basically, whatever the winning bid is, you know, you should be one-third and we should be two-thirds.
And I told him, you know, my upper limit is $2 million.
And guy choked when I told him that.
He said, Monish, you know, I don't think I can do a third of $2 million, but I'm good up to a quarter million.
So I said, okay, here's what we're going to do.
You're going to be capped at a quarter million.
And whatever it goes above that, that's what you're going to pay for your two seats.
So he said that's perfect, great for me.
And then, you know, the bidding petered out at a minuscule 650,000, we didn't even hit the cap for
Guy Spear. It ended up being a tremendous bargain.
So you can see. And then you know how sometimes in stores you have buy one, get one
free. You know, you have a great deal.
this, in hindsight, ended up being buy one and get infinite free.
Because, you know, there was a, what ended up happening is a gazillion lunches with Charlie Munger and
then huge number, large number of Friday afternoons, playing bridge with him and his friends at the

managers and directors and so on. So every year after that, we, Guy and I would
get an invite to that brunch. And, you know, when we would go for that brunch, you know, when we would go for

from 2007 to 2022. And, you know, for pandemic, there was no meetings and all that. But, so
buy one, get infinite free. How can you keep, how can you beat that? And can you tell us

which all this is going to take place, thanks to you. So I owe you a lot, and this is

alive. He was willing to take a bribe to sit down for a meal. Life was great. When Buffett comes

deliver a lot of value. So sometimes I would ask an innocuous question like, hey, you know, there should be three of you.

to meet Charlie for Bridge, Rick used to be there. So then it became like I was playing,

have lunch, you know, the four or five of us used to have lunch together. And I was sitting

and the wife was so pissed off. I mean, she, she was beyond pissed off. She was like,

They want to make some payment to the wife and the mistress and get them to sign over saying,

you know, it's like one of these, you know, old money clubs, whatever.
The first time I met Charlie, I met him at the California club.
It had a very ornette dining room, like huge 40-foot ceilings with Michelangelo type art on the top

So Charlie invited the mistress over for lunch so that he could, you know, schmooze her and talk

So she came directly from work.
And so she came here in a nurse's uniform.

The rest of the members in the club, I mean, they are aghast. Like, what's going on?
Mr. Amonger is one of our esteemed members, and apparently he's meeting a porn star.
For lunch.
Anyway, Charlie said he was able to pacify the women.
They were able to get them to just be cooperated enough to get their deal done.
And then they moved on.
So this is what went on at the lunch and bridge games.
What can I say?
Amazing.
That's so funny.
So I guess you've had the time to talk to Warren, to talk to Charlie, be friends with him.
Alejo, why don't you ask Monish, the question about
how he analyze his companies.
Yeah, Monish, one question I wanted to ask you is a little technical, but I think it's important.
And is how do you read an annual report? Like, what is your schedule? Like, what is your schedule?
Like, you go to the business session, then you read the risk, and, and how do you draw your
circle of competence, like, to pick what annual reports to read on?
Well, I think as far as a circle of competence,
grows to ask the question is to answer it. So if you are wondering whether something is
within your circle of competence or not, the answer is it is not in your circular competence. If something
is within your circular competence, you would know how to value the business. You would know how it makes
makes money. You would know what is a likely trajectory of that business within some ranges and
boundaries. So it depends, it depends on the business. So you would know, you
Usually, my most preferred starting point on a company is to see, you know, as you know, I'm the shameless cloner.
You know, you know. So the first thing I'm trying to ideally try to do is hopefully someone smarter than me already owns the stock.
And hopefully they have made some comments about it.
So the first thing I try to look for is who are the shareholders?
And usually it's, I don't need to look at the shareholders because usually it's, I don't need to look at the
shareholders because usually it is coming through some guy or some fund that I admire
and they have this particular company as a holding. It is ideal for me if there's a write-up on
value investors club. So, you know, there are thousands of write-ups on value investors club and it's
a pretty well-curated site. So when I find a company that's on my radar, the first thing I
look for is, okay, is there a wick write-up? And even if the write-ups are old, I will
print off all the WIC write-ups with all the messages and all the comments, everything on all the
write-ups. That's the first thing I want to read because that is giving me a digested, condensed
view of the business that would take a long time if I just sat and read the annual reports. This is someone who's
already digested a lot of the data and I can ratify that later, but at least it's giving me a head start.
Because the first thing I'm trying to do is anytime I'm looking at a business, I'm looking for a
reason to stop looking and take a pass. So the WIC write-ups are designed to help me get to a point where I say, no, I thought
this might be interesting, but it's not that interesting, so I can let it go. If I get past the WIC write-ups, and I'm still
interested, usually if the company is giving us letters to shareholders, and it appears that those
letters to shareholders are not written by a PR firm. Then not the entire annual
report. I'll have my assistant just make a PDF of all the 20 years of letters, 20, 30 years of letters,
starting with the oldest one. And then I just read the letters, you know, because then I can say,
okay, okay, what were they saying in 95, and then what happened by 2000, what was saying
in 2000, what happened by 2005? I can just see kind of what they were saying,
versus how the trajectory of the business has gone subsequently.
The other interesting thing about reading these letters is, especially reading them in the past.
For example, we know that in 0809, a tsunami is coming.
We know that. So when I'm reading the 2005 letter or 2006 letter or 2007 letter, they don't know that, right?
but I know that. So it's like you're about to go off the, off the cliff.
down the waterfall, but you don't know that. Then they're in the waterfall,
and then they're finally at the bottom. So you know, you can see that whole thing play out in the letter. So
that kind of gives you a view how the company deals with, you know, how resilient the business model is and
adversity. Same thing with the pandemic, right? You know, we can see what 2018, 2019 looks like,
and then suddenly the pandemic hits and kind of, it's throwing some businesses are getting
tailwinds and a lot of them are facing headwinds.
I am still interested in the business after reading the letters.
Then I go to the transcripts. So now the transcripts can be a little bit more. It's actually definitely
not written by a PR firm, right? Because this is actually investors and analysts asking questions
and so on, so forth. So I'm not that interested in the prepared remarks in the transcript
because that would be similar to what's in the reports and the annual reports, because
they're controlling that messaging, but especially the companies that don't write their own letters, et cetera.
I'm really interested in the Q&A.
And of course, I have to sift through stuff because the analysts will ask some stupid question about next quarter,
you know, do you expect to beat by one penny or two pennies and, you know, that sort of thing,
which is not really relevant.
But what I'm looking for is, you know, when different questions are being asked about
the business and they're making different comments. I have the full future
in front of me and just, how did that unfold? Did they under promise and over-deliver? Or did they
over-promise and under-deliver? Or did they over-promise and under-deliver? Or are they conservative? Are they
aggressive? You know, those sorts of things. We can then look at the proxies because that gives me
a good feel for the, you know, stock dilution and comp plans and all of that,
how that is playing out. And then, after all of that, if I'm still interested,
then we start plowing into the financials and, you know, different parts of the annual report,
risk factors, and so on. So that's usually the journey. Do you talk to managers at all
of companies? For the longest time, I didn't talk to managers. Now, especially the ones that are not
in the U.S., basically would not invest without having had plenty of interaction with
the senior management, CEO, and so on. If it's a large U.S. company, there's not
that much you're going to glean. And also, the availability will not, they will not, they will not be very
accessible to you. So you might be able to get to the IR department of, from the large company,
but may not be able to get beyond. Maybe you get to the CFO and so on. I would say
that one of our investments is Micron, you know, I've met Sanjay and I've had some
interaction with their CFO and so on. But I think all of that was really irrelevant to the thesis.
Let's talk about micron. How much of your portfolio does micron weights?
It used to be a lot larger, but due to the, due to our drop in prices in 2020. Well, it might still be
similar proportions, but I would say, I mean, I think at, at one point, micron was around 20, 20% of
the pie, 20, 25% of the pie.
It may be a little bit less right now just because things have come down a bit.
Can you tell us what, what are you seeing in Micron, for example, that makes you invest 25% of your money
in one single company?
Well, we didn't invest 10%.
You know, we have a 10% limit on what we are willing to invest in a single business. So it became
higher because it appreciated it. But I am going to duck that question and I'm going
to probably duck a lot of questions related to what we currently own or what we're looking

inheritances do more harm than good. Well, I think he has a quote. He says, if you are
Jesse Owen's son, you know, Jesse Owens was a sprinter who ran the Olympics in Germany in front of Hitler.

100 meter dashes at the 40 meter line. You know, that's not going to make you a great

And I wanted that, I wanted the full control to go to them at 18. I mean,
they could have taken the money and bought a Ferrari or several Ferraris or gone and

But I felt like we had 18 years to transfer values to them.

you don't need to worry about college.
As it turned out, when they turned 18, we were still doing fine.

They both made choices which were very different than their friends.
They actually focused on what they were truly interested, interested in doing.

I couldn't be proud of them.

So how come you get into that?

most of your money is going to Daxana.
